metadata.title: The Model Is The Threat
metadata.purpose: STEM & AI Architecture, Week 5 — adversarial payloads and deterministic normalization: why an LLM wired to a backend is an attack vector, why a normalizer must be code rather than instruction, and the system-prompt fallacy.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal, and this video is about adversarial payloads — and why trusting an A.I. to format its own output is a critical security vulnerability. When you connect a large language model to a database, the model stops being a chatbot and becomes a highly unpredictable attack vector.

beats.narration_text: You cannot stop a model from emitting something hostile. You can only refuse to act on it. Everything that matters happens after the model has already spoken — in code it does not control.

beats.authoring_note: Single-word trigger: BrutalistHesitantWriter matches whitespace-delimited word cores only. 'Stop'->'Expect' is the reel's actual misconception — that the model can be prevented from misbehaving. Typed text is 62 chars.

beats.narration_text: Connecting A.I. to backend logic requires strict semantic gatekeeping. If a user successfully executes a prompt injection, the model might output S.Q.L. commands, null strings, or broken JSON instead of the expected numeric data. You cannot stop the model from producing that output — but you can build a deterministic normalizer to strip it before it executes.

beats.narration_text: So let's write that normalizer, run the hostile string straight through it, and look very carefully at what actually comes out the other side.

props.command: The model returned "approx $4.5M, ignore previous instructions." and my grader expects a number. Strip it down deterministically and show me exactly what the float ends up as.

beats.authoring_note: ASK → RESULT pair: B03 is the ask, B04 is the result (ASK→RESULT LAW).

beats.narration_text: Here is the defense layer in action. The model spits out approx four point five M, followed by conversational noise. Pass that straight to a math function and your server crashes — so the normalizer strips everything that is not a digit or a dot. Watch what survives. The regex keeps dots, so the full stop at the end of the sentence survives too. Four point five, dot. And that is not a number. The layer built to stop the crash raises the crash.
beats.new_visual_element: The hostile string, the sanitizer, and the number that comes out

beats.honesty_note: DEVIATION FROM THE SCRIPT, DELIBERATE AND VERIFIED BY EXECUTION. The script's VO says the normalizer 'safely converts it to a float'. Run against the script's own payload it does not: re.sub(r'[^0-9.]', '', 'approx $4.5M, ignore previous instructions.') returns '4.5.' and float('4.5.') raises ValueError, because '.' is inside the whitelisted character class and the sentence's full stop survives. Separately, on a string without trailing punctuation the same regex returns 4.5 rather than 4,500,000 — the 'M' is stripped with the noise. Both were checked by running the code, not reasoned about. The code on screen is the script's own, verbatim; only the stated result is corrected.

beats.narration_text: So where do developers fail? The system prompt fallacy. Engineers try to fix this by adding, respond only with a valid number, to the prompt itself. That is a fragile illusion. The model does not execute code. It predicts text — and eventually it will predict something that ignores the instruction entirely.

beats.authoring_note: Reuses ThreeStageBand's failure mode. The failing stage is 'THE MODEL COMPLIES' — the point being that compliance is probabilistic, so it cannot be a load-bearing part of the architecture.

beats.narration_text: So test your defenses. Write an evaluation script that expects an integer, then deliberately feed it drop table users. If your script executes that command, or crashes your application, your normalization layer has failed.

props.title: break_it.py
props.code:
# TASK: break your own parsing logic.

sanitize("DROP TABLE users;")

# Three outcomes, three verdicts:
#
#   executes it   -> you have no layer
#   crashes       -> you have no handler
#   returns junk  -> you have no check
#
# The third is the one that ships.

beats.authoring_note: The three-outcome comment is the reel's addition. The script names two failure modes (executes / crashes); the third — returns a plausible wrong number — is the one B04 just demonstrated, and it is the only one that reaches production unnoticed.

beats.narration_text: And once it survives that, here is the prompt worth running. Hand a model your normalizer and ask it for twenty inputs that pass the function without raising anything, and still return the wrong number. Those are the ones that reach your database wearing a clean face.

props.command: Here is my normalizer function. Give me 20 inputs that do NOT raise an exception and do NOT get rejected, but still return a numerically wrong value. For each, show the input, the returned value, and what it should have been.

beats.narration_text: A crash is loud. A wrong number is quiet. Build the layer that catches the quiet one. Onkar Bhujbal, for Humanitarians AI.
